title: Descartes, reflexes, and the mechanical body (Bridge to AI: the brain as a machine)
text:
CHAPTER 1. EARLIEST IDEAS ABOUT THE BRAIN
SECTION 1.5. DESCARTES, REFLEXES, AND THE MECHANICAL BODY

The body as a machine

Rene Descartes (1596 to 1650) is best known as a philosopher and mathematician: the author of "I think, therefore I am" and the inventor, with Pierre de Fermat, of analytic geometry, which is why we still speak of Cartesian coordinates. But Descartes also wrote about physiology, and his ideas had a large influence on how people thought about the nervous system. For a mechatronics student he is especially interesting, because his central proposal was that the body of an animal, including the human body, is a machine, and that much of its behavior can be explained by mechanical principles without appealing to a soul.

The historical setting matters. In the early seventeenth century, Europe was fascinated by automata: mechanical devices that imitated living things. Royal gardens, such as those at Saint-Germain-en-Laye near Paris, contained hydraulic statues that moved, played music, or appeared to speak when visitors stepped on hidden plates that opened valves. Descartes mentions this kind of device in his writings. Clockwork, pumps, and organ pipes provided a vocabulary for thinking about how things move. William Harvey published his demonstration of the circulation of the blood in 1628, showing that the heart is a pump, and Descartes accepted the circulation (although he explained the heart's motion differently from Harvey, attributing it to heat rather than muscular contraction).

Treatise on Man

Descartes's main physiological work is the Treatise on Man (Traite de l'homme, often called L'Homme). He wrote it in the early 1630s as part of a larger work, The World, but he withheld it from publication, in part after learning of the condemnation of Galileo in 1633. It was published only after his death: first in a Latin translation in 1662 and then in French in 1664. His Passions of the Soul (1649), published in his lifetime, also contains physiological ideas.

In the Treatise on Man, Descartes asks the reader to imagine a statue or machine made by God to resemble a human body as closely as possible. He then explains how such a machine could perform the functions of life: digestion, circulation, breathing, sensation, movement, and even some forms of memory and imagination, using only matter in motion.

His model of the nervous system works roughly like this:

- Nerves are tubes. Inside each nerve are fine threads (filaments) that run from the sense organs to the brain, and the tube also carries "animal spirits," which Descartes describes as a very fine, fast-moving part of the blood, something like a wind or a very subtle flame. These are material, not spiritual, despite the name.
- When a sense organ is stimulated, for example when fire touches the foot, the movement pulls on the filament in the nerve, like pulling a cord that rings a bell. At the brain end, this tug opens a small valve or pore in the inner wall of the ventricles.
- Animal spirits stored in the ventricles flow out through the opened pore into the nerve tube that goes to the appropriate muscles.
- The spirits inflate the muscle, making it swell and shorten, which moves the limb, for example pulling the foot away from the fire.

This is a hydraulic control system. The sensory nerve is a mechanical signal line (a cord), the brain is a manifold of valves, and the motor nerve plus muscle is a hydraulic actuator. Descartes's illustration of a kneeling man pulling his foot from a fire is one of the most famous images in the history of neuroscience, and it is often called the first diagram of a reflex.

Did Descartes discover the reflex?

Historians have debated how far Descartes's account deserves to be called the first theory of the reflex. He did not use the word "reflex" in its modern sense, and the term itself was developed later (Thomas Willis used "reflexion" in a related sense, and in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries physiologists such as Robert Whytt, Jiri Prochaska, and Marshall Hall developed the concept of the reflex arc experimentally). Descartes's mechanism also passes through the brain, whereas we now know that the withdrawal reflex is organized mainly within the spinal cord. But his account does contain the key idea: a stimulus can produce a specific, appropriate movement automatically, through a fixed mechanical pathway, without thought or will. That idea is the core of reflex physiology.

The pineal gland

Descartes needed a place where the soul could interact with the machine, because he did not believe that the rational human mind could be explained mechanically. He chose the pineal gland, a small structure deep in the brain near the ventricles. His reasons were partly anatomical:

- Most brain structures come in pairs, one on each side, while the pineal gland is single. Since we have one unified experience of the world, not two, Descartes argued that the paired images from the two eyes and two halves of the brain must be combined somewhere single.
- He believed the pineal gland was suspended in the ventricles, surrounded by animal spirits, so that small movements of the gland could direct the flow of spirits in different directions, and the flow of spirits could in turn move the gland.

In Descartes's scheme, the soul could tilt the pineal gland slightly, sending spirits into particular nerves and moving the body voluntarily; conversely, sensory signals arriving as patterns of spirit flow could move the gland and so produce perceptions in the soul.

Anatomists soon pointed out problems. The pineal gland is not freely suspended in the ventricles; it is attached to surrounding tissue. Humans are also not the only animals with a pineal gland. Today we know that the pineal gland produces the hormone melatonin and is involved in regulating daily (circadian) rhythms and seasonal biology. It is not the seat of the soul.

Dualism and the mind-body problem

Descartes's overall view is called substance dualism. There are two kinds of thing in the world: extended matter (res extensa), which has size and shape and obeys mechanical laws, and thinking substance (res cogitans), which thinks but has no spatial extent. Animal bodies, including human bodies, are matter. Human minds are thinking substance. Animals, in Descartes's view, have no rational minds and are purely machines. (How literally Descartes meant that animals have no feeling at all is debated by historians; the popular image of Descartes as denying that animals feel pain is probably too simple.)

Dualism leaves a famous puzzle: how can something non-physical push on something physical, or be affected by it? This is the mind-body problem in its classic form. Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia raised exactly this objection in letters to Descartes in 1643, asking how the soul, which is only thinking, could move the bodily spirits. Descartes's replies did not fully satisfy her, or later readers.

Modern neuroscience generally works on the assumption that mental processes are processes in the brain, without a separate non-physical substance. Whether that assumption fully explains conscious experience is still argued about in philosophy. But the working method of neuroscience is the one Descartes recommended for the body: explain as much as possible mechanically, and see how far you get. It has turned out that we can get much further than Descartes expected, because we now explain many of the functions he reserved for the soul, such as language, reasoning, and voluntary choice, in terms of neural mechanisms, at least partly.

Descartes and the machine test

In his Discourse on the Method (1637), Descartes discussed how one could tell a real human from a machine built to look like one. He gave two tests. First, a machine could never use words or signs flexibly, arranging them in different ways to reply appropriately to everything said in its presence, as even the dullest human can. Second, although a machine might do some things as well as or better than us, it would fail at others, because it acts only according to the disposition of its parts and not through understanding; reason is a universal instrument usable in all kinds of situations, while a machine needs a particular arrangement for each particular action.

These two tests are remarkably close to modern debates about AI. The first is a precursor of the Turing test, proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, in which a machine is judged intelligent if its conversation cannot be told apart from a human's. The second is a statement about generality: a machine built for one task cannot handle the open-ended variety of situations that general intelligence can. Large language models now produce flexible replies to a huge range of inputs, which is close to what Descartes said a machine could never do. Whether they do so "through understanding" is exactly the question that philosophers and AI researchers continue to argue about. Descartes's second test, about generality and robustness across all kinds of situations, is closely related to what researchers today call out-of-distribution generalization.

The legacy of the mechanical view

After Descartes, the idea of the body as a machine spread widely. Giovanni Alfonso Borelli (1608 to 1679) applied mechanics to muscle and movement in De motu animalium (published 1680 to 1681), analyzing joints as levers, which is the founding work of biomechanics. In the eighteenth century, Julien Offray de La Mettrie went beyond Descartes in L'homme machine (1747), arguing that humans too are entirely machines, with no separate soul. These ideas fed directly into the experimental physiology of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

At the same time, experiments started to undermine the hydraulic model. If muscles contract because spirits flow into them and inflate them, then a contracting muscle should increase in volume. Experiments in the seventeenth century, including those associated with Jan Swammerdam in the Netherlands and Francis Glisson in England, tested this by contracting muscles in water-filled vessels and looking for a rise in the water level. They found that the volume did not increase noticeably. Swammerdam also showed that a frog nerve-muscle preparation could be made to contract by mechanical stimulation of the nerve, a preparation that would become central to the discovery of bioelectricity. Exactly how these experiments were done and interpreted is described in different ways by historians, but the general result is accepted: the inflation theory of muscle contraction did not survive.

The hydraulic model was gradually replaced. As the next chapter will show, the new candidate was electricity.

Bridge to AI: from hydraulic automata to neural networks

Descartes's nervous system is a sensor, a lookup table, and an actuator. A stimulus pulls a cord, a valve opens, and a pre-set response follows. In robotics, this is a reactive controller. Rodney Brooks's subsumption architecture for mobile robots, developed in the 1980s, deliberately built intelligent-seeming behavior out of layers of simple reactive modules like this, without a central world model. Brooks's robots showed that a surprising amount of useful behavior can come from direct sensor to actuator couplings, exactly the kind of mechanism Descartes proposed for animals.

But Descartes also recognized the limit. A fixed stimulus-response mapping cannot handle new situations. Modern AI tries to overcome this limit in a way Descartes did not consider: by learning the mapping from experience, and by learning internal representations that generalize. A neural network trained by gradient descent is still, in Descartes's terms, "acting according to the disposition of its parts." The difference is that the disposition of the parts is adjusted by data, billions of times, rather than designed by hand. Whether this ever amounts to the "universal instrument" of reason is a deep and open question, and it is one of the threads that run through this book.

There is one more connection. Descartes chose the pineal gland as the single place where everything comes together. Modern neuroscience has found no such single place. Information is distributed across many areas working in parallel, and there is no central screen where perception is "shown" to the self. The philosopher Daniel Dennett called the idea of such a place the "Cartesian theater" and argued against it. Modern deep networks also have no single place where "understanding" happens; meaning is spread across many units and layers. Both brains and networks force us to think about distributed representations, a theme we will meet again in the chapters on localization, on neural coding, and on AI.

Summary

- Descartes proposed that animal and human bodies are machines, explained by matter in motion.
- His Treatise on Man (published after his death, 1662 and 1664) describes a hydraulic nervous system with cords in nerves, valves in the brain, and animal spirits inflating muscles.
- His image of a man withdrawing his foot from fire is a famous early picture of a reflex mechanism, although the reflex concept was developed experimentally later.
- He located the interaction of the soul and the body in the pineal gland, which we now know regulates circadian rhythms through melatonin.
- His dualism created the classic mind-body problem, raised sharply by Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia.
- His tests for distinguishing humans from machines anticipated the Turing test and the modern problem of generalization.
- Experiments on muscle volume undermined the hydraulic model, preparing the way for bioelectricity.
